summary: Defines the Start TLS operation for LDAPv3, which lets a client and server turn an ordinary LDAP connection into an encrypted one. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4510, RFC 4511 and RFC 4513.

plainLanguage.summary: Start TLS is a way of adding encryption to an LDAP connection that is already open, rather than connecting to a separate port for it. The client asks for it with a special message, the server says yes or no, and if it says yes the two sides then negotiate TLS on the same connection before anything else is sent.

subtitle: The operation that turns an ordinary LDAP connection into an encrypted one.

tldr.problem: LDAP servers often need to authenticate their clients and sometimes need the traffic to be confidential, but a client may not know that when it opens the connection.
tldr.mechanism: The Start TLS operation is an LDAP extended request with a fixed object identifier. The client sends it, the server agrees, and the two then run a TLS handshake over the same TCP connection before any further LDAP traffic.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2830 is a Proposed Standard from May 2000 and has been obsoleted by RFC 4511, RFC 4510 and RFC 4513, which cover the LDAP protocol and its security.

today: RFC 2830 is a Proposed Standard from May 2000, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 4511, RFC 4510 and RFC 4513, which cover the LDAP protocol, its framework and its authentication; the unit metadata also lists RFC 3377 as updating it. The RFC itself notes that the security gained through the Start TLS operation is gained by the use of TLS itself, and that the operation on its own provides no additional security.

sections.title: What the Start TLS Operation Does
sections.content:
This RFC defines the Start Transport Layer Security operation for LDAP. The operation provides for TLS to be established within an LDAP association, and is defined in terms of an LDAP extended request. It is the LDAP equivalent of the way other protocols upgrade a plain connection in place.

Two points follow from the design. The first is that the operation is negotiated, so the client learns whether the server is willing before it commits anything. The second is that it happens on an existing connection, so the client may already have bound, or may not have bound at all, and the server may already have asked for a certificate. The RFC spells out the effect on the client's authorization identity in a separate section, because establishing TLS does not by itself change who the client is.

The RFC is careful to note what the operation does not do. It adds no security of its own: everything gained comes from TLS itself. It does not protect the data held by the directory server, and it does not protect the data from the server's own administrators. Once established, TLS provides confidentiality and integrity for the operations and data in transit over the LDAP association, and only if both implementations support it and negotiate it.
sections.plainLanguage: The operation is a request and an answer, followed by an ordinary TLS handshake. It does not itself encrypt anything; all the security comes from TLS.

sections.title: The Start TLS Request and Response
sections.content:
A client performs the operation by transmitting an LDAP protocol data unit containing an extended request whose request name is the object identifier 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.20037. The extended request is defined as an application 23 structure with a request name field and an optional request value field. The request value field is absent for a Start TLS request. The client must not send any further protocol data units on that connection until it receives the extended response.

The server must answer with an extended response, which is an application 24 structure holding the components of an LDAP result, an optional response name and an optional response field. The response name must be set to the same string as in the request, and the response field is absent. The server must set the result code to either success or one of the other values the RFC lists.

If the result code is success, the server is willing and able to negotiate TLS. The RFC separates this from the other case deliberately: the client learns that the handshake may begin, and then the client, having stopped transferring LDAP requests, must either begin a TLS negotiation or close the connection. From that point the client sends records of the TLS record protocol directly over the underlying transport connection to start the negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The request carries a fixed number that says what it is, and no data of its own. The reply carries the same number back and a status. After a success the message traffic stops and the two sides speak TLS instead.

sections.title: Sequencing the Operation
sections.content:
The client may send the Start TLS extended request at any time after establishing an LDAP association, with three exceptions. It must not send it if TLS is currently established on the connection, if a multi-stage SASL negotiation is in progress, or if there are any LDAP operations outstanding. Breaking any of these rules gives a result code of operationsError. The client may have performed a bind before sending the request, or may not have bound yet.

If the client did not establish TLS before sending other requests, and the server requires TLS for a particular request, the server must reject that request with a confidentialityRequired or strongAuthRequired result. The client may then send a Start TLS request or close the connection.

After a successful extended response, the client, which has ceased transferring LDAP requests, must either begin a TLS negotiation or close the connection. The TLS version is negotiated as part of the TLS handshake protocol, which is outside this document. Once the TLS connection is established, both parties must individually decide whether to continue, based on the privacy level achieved; ascertaining it is implementation-dependent and is done by talking to the local TLS implementation. If either side decides the level of authentication or privacy is not high enough, it should close the TLS connection gracefully as soon as the negotiation completes.

The client may then assert a specific authorization identity by sending a bind request that names the EXTERNAL SASL mechanism. It must also check the server's identity: the client must compare the hostname it used to open the connection against the name in the server's certificate, and must not use the server's canonical DNS name or any other derived form of name. If a subjectAltName extension of type dNSName is present it should be used as the source of the identity, matching is case-insensitive, and the wildcard character is allowed but applies only to the left-most name component. If the hostname does not match, a user-oriented client should either notify the user or terminate the connection and report the server's identity as suspect; an automated client should close the connection and log an error.

Finally, the client must refresh any cached server capabilities information, such as what it read from the server's root DSE, once TLS is established. That protects against an active intermediary that altered the capabilities before TLS began. The server may advertise different capabilities afterwards.
sections.plainLanguage: There are rules about when the request may be sent, and rules about what the client must do once TLS is up: check that the certificate really names the host it asked for, and throw away anything it learned before the connection was protected.

sections.title: Failure Codes and Closing the Connection
sections.content:
When the extended request does not succeed, the result code says why. operationsError means the client broke one of the sequencing rules, for example asking for TLS when it is already established, and the server must return it in that case. protocolError means TLS is not supported or the message structure was wrong; a server that does not support TLS, whether by design or by current configuration, must set this code or referral, and if it returns a referral it must include an actual referral value. The client's session is unaffected, and it may proceed with any LDAP operation or close the connection. unavailable means the server supports TLS but cannot establish it, for example because the certificate server is not responding, it cannot reach its TLS implementation, or it is shutting down; the client may retry, proceed with another operation, or close the connection.

Either side may terminate the TLS connection by sending a closure alert, which leaves the LDAP association intact. Before closing, the client must either wait for outstanding LDAP operations to complete or explicitly abandon them. After sending a closure alert the initiator must discard any TLS messages until it receives an alert from the other party, and afterwards it may send and receive LDAP messages again. The other party, on receiving a closure alert, must immediately transmit one in reply. Either side may also close everything abruptly by dropping the underlying TCP connection, and a server may first send a notice of disconnection.
sections.plainLanguage: When the server says no, the code says whether it does not support TLS, is busy, or the client broke the rules. Either side can also end the encrypted part while keeping the LDAP connection open.

sections.title: What Establishing TLS Does to the Client's Identity
sections.content:
Establishing TLS does not by itself change who the client is. Any previously established authentication and authorization identities must remain in force, including anonymous state, and this holds even when the server asks the client for a certificate during the TLS negotiation.

A client may nevertheless ask for a different identity to be used. It can do so implicitly, by sending a bind request that names the EXTERNAL SASL mechanism and leaves out the optional credentials string; the server then derives the authorization identity from the identity in the client's TLS credentials according to local policy. Or it can do so explicitly, by including a credentials string built as RFC 2829 describes, which is how a proxy asks for the privileges of the identity it is acting for.

In either case the server must check that the client's authentication identity from its TLS credentials is permitted to be mapped to the asserted authorization identity, and must reject the bind with an invalidCredentials result if it is not. If no TLS session was established, or no other external source of credentials exists, or the server did not request the client's credentials during the TLS session, the EXTERNAL bind must fail with an inappropriateAuthentication result. After such a failure the association loses its authentication and authorization state and becomes anonymous, although the TLS connection itself is unaffected and the server may end it.

Closing the TLS connection must move the LDAP association to an anonymous authentication and authorization state, whatever state was established over TLS and whatever state existed before it.
sections.plainLanguage: Turning on encryption does not log you in. To claim an identity from a certificate, the client has to say so with a bind, and the server has to agree that the certificate may stand for that identity.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The goals of using TLS with LDAP are to ensure connection confidentiality and integrity, and optionally to provide authentication. All the security gained through the Start TLS operation is gained by the use of TLS itself; the operation on its own provides nothing extra.

The use of TLS does not provide or ensure confidentiality or non-repudiation for the data held by an LDAP directory server, and it does not protect the data from inspection by the server's administrators. The level of security depends directly on the quality of the TLS implementation and on the style of its use.

There is one trap the RFC points out. An active-intermediary attacker can remove the Start TLS operation from the supportedExtension attribute of the root DSE, so a client that believes TLS is available never tries it. Both parties should therefore independently ascertain and agree the security level achieved once TLS is established and before using the connection, because the level might have been negotiated down to plaintext. Clients should either warn the user when the level achieved does not give confidentiality or integrity, or be configurable to refuse to proceed without an acceptable level.

The RFC also says that implementors should protect credentials and other confidential data where the TLS implementation does not already do so, and that server implementors should let administrators choose whether and when connection confidentiality, integrity or client authentication through TLS are required.
sections.plainLanguage: The big risk is that an attacker in the middle convinces the client that TLS is not even available, so the client never asks for it. Both ends therefore have to check what they actually got, and the client has to be able to refuse to carry on if it is not good enough.

viz.caption: THE RESULT CODES OF THE START TLS REQUEST (RFC 2830)

items.label: Success
items.desc: The server is willing and able to negotiate TLS. The client must then begin the negotiation or close the connection.

items.label: Operations error
items.desc: The client violated one of the sequencing rules, for example asking again while TLS is already established. The server must return this code in that case.

items.label: Protocol error
items.desc: TLS is not supported, or the PDU structure was incorrect.

items.label: Referral
items.desc: This server does not do TLS; the result must carry an actual referral value. The client may proceed with any LDAP operation or close the connection.

items.label: Unavailable
items.desc: The server supports TLS but cannot establish it, for example because its certificate server is not responding or it is shutting down.

viz.caption: THE EFFECTS OF ESTABLISHING TLS (RFC 2830, SECTION 5)

items.title: Identity unchanged
items.text: Any identity already established stays in force, including anonymous state, even if the server asked for a certificate.

items.title: Assert an identity
items.text: A bind with the EXTERNAL mechanism lets the client ask the server to use the identity from its TLS credentials.

items.title: Check the server
items.text: The client must compare the hostname it used with the name in the server's certificate, case-insensitively, with a wildcard only in the left-most label.

items.title: Refresh capabilities
items.text: Cached server capabilities must be fetched again once TLS is established, because an attacker may have altered them earlier.
